question: Which song by The Beatles starts with a chord jump from the tonic to the minor fitfh chord?

4.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Penny Lane. The intro is the giveaway — the track is set up in D major and the very first two bars are built around a dramatic tritone jump from the D major tonic straight to an Ab major chord, the flat-five/minor-fifth relation. That sudden drop from the home chord into the dissonant fifth is what gives the opening its bright, slightly unsettled brass fanfare feel before the verse settles in, and it’s the same kind of tonic-to-flat-five leap people usually associate with the Revolver/Magical Mystery Tour era.

6.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Penny Lane. The intro is the one everyone remembers for that wide opening leap. After the piccolo trumpet fanfare the band lands on a clear D major tonic, and then immediately jumps down a fifth to the A minor chord that defines the verse’s minor fifth colour. It’s that tonic-to-v drop that gives Penny Lane its slightly unsettled, almost circus-like start before the brass comes back in, and it’s the same kind of dramatic intervallic leap that people usually associate with the late-1966/early-1967 studio experiments.

3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The textbook example that is normally quoted is A Day In The Life.

The piece is in A major. The famous piano intro / first verse is launched on a huge tonic A major and the harmony which the vocal line is first heard over is the v chord of the key, E minor, a perfect 5th below the tonic and the minor-mode 5th degree of A major. In other words the opening phrase is heard as

I – v
A major → E minor

in A major, the tonic leaping down a fifth to its minor dominant. That I–v leap, tonic to the minor fifth-degree chord, is the dissonant, open-fifth colour that gives the opening of “A Day In The Life” its characteristic jump. The same I–v tonic-to-minor-fifth opening colour is the one that is usually cited for the Strawberry Fields Forever / A Day In The Life family of Lennon/McCartney experiments, with A Day In The Life being the canonical case.

If the tritone reading of “tonic to the minor fifth = a 6-semitone root move” is intended, the Beatles’ most often quoted tritone opening is I Am The Walrus, which opens with a C♯/F♯ area tonic and immediately moves a tritone to the ♭V/G♯ family harmony that underlies the “I am the walrus” vocal entry.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: In the Beatles’ 1960-64 catalogue the I–v opening is the
text-book I–v jump. The clearest textbook example is Help! and the
song it is built on in the same key, I Should Have Known Better /
Can’t Buy Me Love.

In A major the song opens on the tonic A major and in the same bar the
band lands on E minor. In A major E is the 5th degree of the scale and
the chord is minor, i.e. the v chord, the tonic-to-the-minor-fifth
motion I → v. E minor is a fifth up from, and a 7 semitone/ 7 note
diatonic fifth up from, the tonic A. The same I–v jump is heard at the
very start of the A-major verse of I Should Have Known Better and of the
E-major verse of Can’t Buy Me Love – E major tonic to B minor v – and it
is the convention that is normally quoted as the Beatles’ I-to-minor-fifth
opening. 

That I–v tonic-to-dominant-minor leap is the one that is usually cited,
e.g. Help! A – E m,  I Should Have Known Better A – E m, Can’t Buy Me Love
E – B m, Ticket to Ride D – A m, etc., the prototype being Help! in A major.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: In the Beatles canon the textbook example of an opening I → v
root movement is the A-major opening of Strawberry Fields Forever.

In the recorded version the song is heard in A major. The first heard
harmony is the tonic A major, A–C♯–E, and the very next change the
band makes is to the chord built on the fifth degree of the A-major
scale, E minor, E–G–B. E minor is the v–chord of A major, i.e. the
minor fifth chord of the tonic, a perfect-fifth root movement A → E
down a fifth / up a fourth. That I → v jump is the distinctive tonic-to-
minor-fifth opening that is normally quoted for the track and which is
often described in the popular literature as a tonic → minor-fifth
chord jump. The same I–v colour is the one that gives the opening of
the song its characteristic unsettled, “wrong” fifth feel before the
form settles into the familiar A–E–F♯m–D progression.

In popular-theory shorthand the jump that is meant is the I – bV tritone jump
that is the root a minor 5th / diminished 5th up from the tonic.  It is the
E – B♭ / E – B♭m jump that opens the middle-eight-ish / verse material of
the late-period rockers.

The textbook example is the E-major opening of *Come Together* – and in the
same family the E-major opening of *Helter Skelter* / *I Want You (She’s So
Heavy)*.  The song is in E major and the very first melodic / harmonic
motion is the tonic E-major triad to a chord whose root is a tritone /
minor 5th up from E, B♭/B♭m.  In the recording it is heard as the
characteristic E → B♭/B♭m riff that begins the tune, i.e. a tonic-to-flat-
five/minor-fifth jump.  The jump is the one that is normally quoted as the
Beatles’ textbook I → bV tritone opening.  The same move is most often
demonstrated with the E → B♭ tonic-to-minor-fifth opening of *Helter
Skelter* / *I Want You (She’s So Heavy)*, the classic late-Beatles
tritone tonic jump.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the confusion here is the word “minor fifth” and that’s what’s pulling the discussion in different directions.

When musicians talk about a jump from the tonic to the *minor fifth chord* they are referring to an interval size, not just the diatonic v chord. A minor fifth / diminished fifth is a tritone, six semitones, root up bV. That’s the flat-five / tritone jump that gives those late-60s openings their characteristic unsettled feel.

Strawberry Fields Forever, A Day In The Life, Help! etc. are all the classic I – v perfect-fifth root moves: A major to E minor, A major to E minor, A major to E minor. A to E is a perfect fifth root movement, seven semitones. E minor is the v chord of A major, i.e. the minor *quality* fifth degree, but the interval between the roots is a perfect fifth, not a minor fifth. The same applies to Colleague 1’s Help! / I Should Have Known Better examples and Colleague 3’s A Day In The Life reading. That’s a tonic-to-minor-quality-five-degree move, not a tonic-to-minor-fifth-interval move.

The recorded tonic-to-bV tritone opening everyone actually cites is Penny Lane. The track is set up in D major. The piccolo trumpet fanfare lands squarely on D major and the harmony then drops immediately to Ab major, the flat-five / diminished-fifth / tritone relation to D. That is a six-semitone root move D → Ab, the textbook I – bV minor-fifth jump and the reason the intro sounds so bright and slightly wrong before the verse settles. It’s the same family of move that Colleague 2 is describing for Come Together / Helter Skelter, where the E major riff moves to Bb / Bbm, a tritone away.

That’s why Penny Lane keeps coming up as the canonical example. It is literally a tonic chord jumping a minor fifth / tritone up to the flat-five chord in the opening bars, not a diatonic v colour.

Colleagues 1, 3 and 5 are describing the very real Beatles I → v move: tonic to the minor triad built on the fifth degree of the key. That’s Help! A → Em, A Day In The Life A → Em, Strawberry Fields Forever A → Em, Ticket to Ride D → Am, etc. It is a perfect-fifth root movement, 7 semitones, to a minor triad on the fifth scale degree. That’s a useful and often quoted colour, and Strawberry Fields is a textbook I→v opening.

The phrasing “tonic to the minor fifth chord” is normally used in Beatles literature with the interval reading, i.e. a root move by a diminished/minor fifth, a tritone / flat five, six semitones. That is a different move from I→v. A → E is a perfect fifth, not a minor fifth interval.

That is why the canonical example people point to for a tonic-to-bV / tritone jump is the brass fanfare opening of Penny Lane. The tune is set up in D major and the first harmonic gesture is D major straight to the flat-five/tritone sonority a tritone away before the verse settles. It’s the textbook Revolver/Magical Mystery Tour tonic-to-minor-fifth interval jump and it’s the same family Colleague 2 mentions with the E → B♭/B♭m opening of Come Together / Helter Skelter / I Want You.

If we keep the interval reading, the I→v examples, including the A → Em of Strawberry Fields Forever, are perfect-fifth root movements, not minor-fifth interval jumps. The tritone opening that actually fits the wording is the Penny Lane / Come Together family.
public_text.3:
The textbook I → v opening that is quoted again and again in the Beatles literature is the A-major opening.

Help! is the prototype of the move. The song is in A major. The band comes in on the tonic A major and in the same opening bar/ phrase lands on the chord built on the 5th degree of the key, E minor E–G–B. That is the diatonic v chord of A major, i.e. a perfect-fifth root move tonic → the minor fifth-degree chord, conventionally described in the popular literature as a tonic-to-minor-fifth jump.

The same I → v colour is the one that is normally cited for the A-major opening of Strawberry Fields Forever, and for the same move in the same key in I Should Have Known Better A → E m, and in parallel keys Can’t Buy Me Love E → B m and Ticket to Ride D → A m. It is that perfect-fifth, minor-quality dominant, v, movement that gives those openings their characteristic unsettled “wrong fifth” feel.

If the “minor fifth” is taken in the interval sense, i.e. a root move of a diminished/minor 5th = a tritone, the late-period tonic → bV jump that is normally quoted is the E → B♭/B♭m opening of Come Together / Helter Skelter / I Want You, and the classic Revolver-era tritone fanfare example is Penny Lane D major → A♭ major in the brass intro.

The move that is normally talked about as a tonic-to-“minor-fifth” move in the Beatles literature is the root a diminished/minor 5th up from the tonic, i.e. the I → bV tritone. 

That is the move that is written about for the Revolver/Magical Mystery Tour brass/fanfare openings. The clearest textbook case is

Penny Lane – D major → A♭ major.

The track is set up in D major and the very first two bars of the piccolo-trumpet fanfare are built on the dramatic tritone/major-minor fifth jump

D major  = I
A♭ major = bV

which is heard as the tonic leaping a minor 5th/diminished 5th up to its flat-five. It is the same intervallic family that is quoted for the E-major openings of Come Together/Helter Skelter/I Want You , E → B♭/B♭m, i.e. tonic to a chord whose root is a minor 5th/tritone up from the tonic.

Remark on terminology: if “the minor fifth chord” is taken in the diatonic sense, i.e. the chord built on the 5th degree of the major scale which is minor, the move is the textbook I → v perfect-fifth root movement. The Beatles’ prototype for that is the A-major opening

Help! – A major → E minor

and the same I–v colour that is quoted for I Should Have Known Better/Can’t Buy Me Love, Ticket to Ride D→A m and the Lennon/McCartney experiments Strawberry Fields Forever A→E m and A Day In The Life A→E m. The A→E m I–v jump is the one that is normally cited as the Beatles’ tonic-to-minor-fifth-degree opening.

The split in round 0 is really a terminology split.

* I → v = tonic to the minor chord built on the 5th scale degree, root movement a perfect 5th. That is the “tonic to the minor fifth degree” move that is normally quoted in Beatles literature. 
* I → bV = tonic to a chord whose root is a minor 5th / tritone away from the tonic.

The I → v reading is the one the majority of the round 0 posts are using for “tonic to the minor fifth chord”. Under that reading the prototype is the A major opening.

Help! is the canonical textbook instance. The song is set up in A major and the very first harmonic motion is heard as

A major  →  E minor

A is the tonic, E is the 5th degree of A major and the chord that is actually played is the minor v. The same I → v colour is then quoted for the A-major verse of I Should Have Known Better, for the E-major verse of Can’t Buy Me Love E → Bm, for Ticket to Ride D → Am and for the A-major family Strawberry Fields Forever / A Day In The Life A → Em.

Strawberry Fields Forever is often put forward as the A → Em exemplar and A Day In The Life is quoted in the same family, the three songs being essentially the same I → v tonic-to-minor-fifth colour with Help! being the earliest and most widely cited prototype.

On the tritone reading the Penny Lane discrepancy has to be cleared up. Colleague 6 reads Penny Lane as D major → A minor, i.e. I → v. The recorded intro is in fact the famous Revolver/Magical Mystery Tour tritone fanfare D major → A♭ major, a tonic to flat-five / minor-fifth root move in the bV sense. That is the same family as the E → B♭/B♭m opening of Come Together / Helter Skelter / I Want You which is the textbook I → bV tritone jump.

So with the conventional “minor fifth chord = v” reading the consensus example is Help!, A major → E minor, with Strawberry Fields Forever / A Day In The Life as the same I → v colour. If the question is intended in the tritone / flat-five sense, the Beatles’ textbook I → bV opening is Come Together, E major → B♭, and Penny Lane is the classic D → A♭ illustration of that move.
